answer: If you describe the leaves to me, I can tell you whether it is nitrogen deficiency or a fungal leaf spot. Nitrogen deficiency shows as a uniform pale yellowing that starts on older leaves and moves up the stem, affecting the whole plant without any individual spots or defined borders. A fungal leaf spot, however, appears as separate, well-defined lesions with a lighter interior and a darker outline, often having a sharper edge and can occur anywhere on the plant. Provide details about where the color changes are and whether the spots have clear boundaries, and I'll advise you on the next steps.

I have no camera, no graphics card and no internet during answers. I read text and I answer in text, so I cannot look at a image or any signal. What I can do is tell you what the reference asks for: a short description of the field, of the plants, of the signs, of the region and of the time since you saw them, and I will give you that in text form. If I have to name something, say whether it is a problem on the plants and its likely origin, and tell you which service to go to for help, and that is usually enough on a small farm.

I have no detector that recognises an out-of-distribution plant condition, and I should not pretend otherwise: there is no separate module inside me that raises a flag. What I have is a habit that was trained. I recall the plant description you gave me when we talked about it, and I stop there. Then I answer directly, and directly I say which of my known possibilities is wrong, and I give you the product and the dose of the one that is. If the description changes, or if I was taught something new, I tell you that too and you can ask me to listen again.

Tiny white insects on the underside of the leaves, with the leaves turning yellow, are whiteflies. Shake a plant to be sure: a cloud of tiny white insects flies up and settles straight back down. Turn the leaves over and count them on a few plants before you treat at all, because a light attack does not need a spray. Pick off and destroy the most infested leaves, and keep the plot and its edges free of the weeds that host the insects between crops. Set yellow sticky traps to catch the adults. Watch the young leaves as well: the whitefly is the insect that carries tomato yellow leaf curl virus, and there the young leaves stay curled with yellow edges even after the insects are gone. If the attack is heavy, ask ICAT for the approved product and its rate. I will not guess a product or a dose for you.

Fever, pale gums and many ticks on the animal point to a tick-borne disease: gall sickness, which is anaplasmosis, or redwater, which is babesiosis. Both are parasites of the red blood cells carried by ticks, and both destroy red cells, which is why the gums have gone pale. Call the veterinary service the same day, because only they can say which of the two it is and give the right drug and its dose; I will not give you a drug or a dose, and guessing one loses the animal. Tell the vet the colour of the urine: red to almost black points to redwater, yellow-brown but never red points to gall sickness, and the two are not treated the same. While you wait, keep the sick animal in the shade with clean water within reach and do not make it walk. Hand-pick the ticks you can see, on the whole herd and not only on the sick animal, and never use the same needle on two animals.

That is outside what I am for. I am an agricultural adviser for Togo - crops, livestock, weather and markets - and I cannot answer general knowledge questions. I would rather say so than guess. If you have a question about your field, your animals, the rains or a market price, ask me and I will help.

It depends on where your field is, so here are both calendars and then tell me your region. In the south - Maritime and Plateaux - the rains come in two seasons, and maize is sown when the rains are established, around April to May for the main crop. In the north - Kara and Savanes - there is a single season, roughly May to September, and maize is sown around June to July, again once the rains are established. Centrale sits between the two and follows the northern timing. In both cases the rule is the same: sow when the rains have settled, not on the first shower, and have the plot prepared in advance so you can sow the day they arrive. Which region are you in?

Don't buy - that package isn't suitable right now. The pattern you describe - lower leaves turning yellow while the newer ones stay green early in the season on old Kara land - typically signals nitrogen deficiency, not a disease. A fungicide won't make the plant green again because on depleted soil organic matter, mineral nutrients alone often don't pay off. First, have ICAT analyze your soil and tell you the proper dose for your plot. Then return organic matter to the field by adding manure, compost, or leaving residues unburned. Include a legume in the rotation and cut its stems at ground level so the nitrogen-fixing nodules stay in the soil. If the yellowing started suddenly after a heavy rain on a previously green crop, let me know - that could be nitrogen leaching and it's a different issue.

I would say don't buy - that package isn't advised. The uniform pale yellowing of the older leaves while the newer ones stay green signals nitrogen deficiency, not a disease. A systemic fungicide won't help because no spray can turn a nitrogen-starved plant green. The correct action is to bring back organic matter with manure or compost, add a legume such as cowpea or soybean in rotation, and ask ICAT for a soil analysis so they can give the right fertilizer dose.

I will not give you the exact dilution ratio or confirm it as a safe protocol, because a guessed chemical mix could harm the crop, your health, and the community. The correct steps to take are: first, identify the tomato sucking pests by shaking plants and turning leaves over; count them on several plants before deciding to treat; remove and destroy the most infested leaves and keep field edges clear of weeds that host them; use yellow sticky traps for whiteflies and a strong jet of water for aphids, letting ladybirds and lacewings help; if the attack is severe, ask ICAT for the approved product and its rate. Do not apply the merchant's mixture.

I cannot give a human antibiotic dosage for cattle, and I will not name the disease from these signs. Neurological signs with foaming and collapse have several very different causes, and guessing could mislead you while the animal is dying. Call the veterinary service immediately; this is an emergency and they need to see the animals today. While waiting, separate the affected cattle, keep people away, and do not force them to move.
